sentences.text: This animal measured about 4 meters in length, with a small, elongated head roughly twenty centimeters long. Its skull was low in side view, triangular from above, and longer than it was wide, resembling earlier ornithischians.
The body was lightly armoured with long horizontal rows of keeled oval scutes extending along the neck, back, and tail.

James Harrison discovered fossils in the Black Ven cliffs near Charmouth and Lyme Regis during the 1850s. In 1858, he and Henry Norris sent fragmentary limb bones to Professor Richard Owen at the British Museum in London.
Richard Owen named and described the genus Scelidosaurus in 1859 following these initial finds.
It was largely quadrupedal and fed on low scrubby plants, which were bitten off by its small head and processed in a large gut.

Owen suggested in 1861 that it was a fish-eater that partially lived in the sea and might have been ovoviviparous due to its size and presumed marine lifestyle, though these views differ from modern ideas.
Owen placed the animal in the Dinosauria in 1861, and Thomas Henry Huxley validly named the family Scelidosauridae in 1869.
It is considered one of the oldest and most primitive thyreophorans, and Scelidosaurus harrisonii is the only currently recognized species.
The animal lived during the Early Jurassic epoch, specifically the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian ages, approximately 191 million years ago.

Fossils have been found in the Charmouth Mudstone Formation near Charmouth in Dorset, England, including a partial juvenile skeleton dating to the early Pliensbachian, approximately 190 million years ago.

Current evidence suggests Scelidosaurus is the most derived of known basal thyreophorans, being either closely related to Ankylosauria or to the Stegosauria+Ankylosauria clade. It is debated whether a misidentified knee joint belongs to Scelidosaurus or to a member of the Coelophysoidea or Neoceratosauria. David Jay Simmons described fossils from the Sinemurian-age Lower Lufeng Formation as a potential second species, Scelidosaurus oehleri, in 1965, initially placing it in the genus Tatisaurus. Spencer G. Lucas reassigned S. oehleri to Scelidosaurus in 1996, but this view is not accepted, and the species is now recognized as Tatisaurus.
